Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette: Elena Rodriguez remembers the compound walls closing in as the patrols tightened their net. The sharp, familiar tang of aguardiente clung to the border guards as they directed the line of refugees with barked instructions. She watched a man in a crisp olive uniform gesture toward the processing tents, his movements sudden and heavy. Elena had braced herself, expecting another wave of footsteps, another shout that would send her scurrying into the shadows. When the memory surfaces now, it arrives with the same cadence: she hears the guards’ voices echoing in her head, clear and distinct, just as they had been that evening. The details remain locked in place—the cracked pavement, the metallic groan of the gates, the heavy wool of her coat. She does not just recall the event; she relives its texture, and the weight of it often stops her mid-step, leaving her breathless until the moment passes. In the years that followed, Elena had come to believe the world remained as precarious as that night. She was certain that danger could materialize without warning, and she began to distrust the ease of those around her, wondering what motives lay beneath their smiles. What frightened her most was the quiet uncertainty of her own reflection; she looked in the mirror and felt like a stranger wearing her own skin, unsure of who she was or how to act. To steady herself, she developed habits that made sense in their own logic. She dwelled on the night, replaying the decisions she might have made differently, certain that one different choice would have kept her family intact. When the past pressed close, she would fill the silence with loud television or blast her playlist until the sounds from her childhood faded into the background. She learned to position herself carefully, always choosing seats near exits or against solid walls, ensuring she was shielded from whatever might approach. Now, as a prison guard in a sprawling state facility, her daily environment mirrors the landscape of her fear. The corridors echo with the clipped tones of officers, and the scent of alcohol from the break room drifts past her desk, catching her off guard. When a supervisor approaches and issues a direct order, Elena’s shoulders tense, her breath catching as if she is being called to attention once more. She notices the uniforms around her, the structured authority in their posture, and she finds herself stepping back, giving them space rather than meeting them head-on. Unexpected movement near her workspace sends a quick ripple through her; she turns sharply, assessing the threat before she realizes it is only a colleague reaching for a file. She has started to react as though the past is breathing down her neck, even on quiet shifts when the doors are locked and the yard is still. Her careful positioning and heightened alertness have reshaped her workdays, turning routine patrols into moments of sustained vigilance. The quiet accumulation of these patterns has left Elena weary. Her husband notices the distance she keeps, the way she scans the room before sitting down, the way she sometimes stops mid-sentence when a voice from the past rises in her mind. Her PCL5 score reflects the weight of her symptoms, but it is the daily reality that finally brought her to the clinic. She came on a Thursday after a routine head count triggered such a sudden wave of overwhelm that she had to step outside, leaning against the brick wall until her breathing slowed. She no longer wants to live in a state of perpetual readiness. She hopes to understand why the world feels so heavy, and what she might do to stop bracing for a danger that is no longer there.
